sentences.text: Here is a right triangle. Its legs are three and four, and its hypotenuse is five — the most famous triple there is.
sentences.spoken: Here is a right triangle. Its legs are three and four, and its hypotenuse is five — the most famous triple there is.

sentences.text: The theorem says the square on the hypotenuse equals the two squares on the legs, added together. {squares_draw}But why?
sentences.spoken: The theorem says the square on the hypotenuse equals the two squares on the legs, added together. But why?

sentences.text: Take four copies of that triangle. {four_copies}They pack into a square of side seven — three plus four — in two different ways.
sentences.spoken: Take four copies of that triangle. They pack into a square of side seven — three plus four — in two different ways.

sentences.text: Packed one way, {pack_a}the four triangles leave two squares: side three, and side four.
sentences.spoken: Packed one way, the four triangles leave two squares: side three, and side four.

sentences.text: Packed the other way, {pack_b}the same four triangles leave one square: side five — the hypotenuse.
sentences.spoken: Packed the other way, the same four triangles leave one square: side five — the hypotenuse.

sentences.text: Same square of side seven. Same four triangles. {both_shown}So what is left must be equal: nine plus sixteen equals twenty five.
sentences.spoken: Same square of side seven. Same four triangles. So what is left must be equal: nine plus sixteen equals twenty five.

sentences.text: Three squared plus four squared equals five squared. {equation_lands}Nine plus sixteen, twenty five. Every right triangle, always.
sentences.spoken: Three squared plus four squared equals five squared. Nine plus sixteen, twenty five. Every right triangle, always.
